Chapter Seven: Adapting the Model to Leadership and Influence.
You know, leadership isn’t about having a single style that fits every situation. The best leaders are the ones who can read the room, shift gears, and adjust how they lead to fit what their team needs in the moment. That’s where the color model really shines—it gives you a hands-on toolkit for this kind of flexible, adaptive leadership.
So, how do you lead people with different color styles?
With Reds, it’s all about clear goals and real authority. Trust them to handle things their way, celebrate their wins, and try not to step on their toes or double-check every move. Micromanaging? That’s a big no for most Reds.
When you’re leading Yellows, bring out their creativity and keep things positive. Celebrate successes, and let their enthusiasm shine—just make sure you give them enough structure to keep moving forward, but not so much that you put out their spark.
For Greens, focus on creating a supportive, steady environment. Let them be part of decisions, give them plenty of stability, and avoid springing sudden changes on them or criticizing them in front of the group. They really shine when they feel safe and included.
And with Blues, details matter. Set the bar high, respect their need for accuracy, and give them all the information they need. Let them take their time to analyze before deciding—if you rush them, you’ll only get pushback.
Think about the last time you rolled out something new at work. An adaptive leader might inspire Yellows with a bold vision, make Greens feel secure with a step-by-step plan, motivate Reds with a big challenge, and win Blues over by showing thorough research. It’s about finding what lights up each person.
Now, let’s talk about building a culture where adaptability isn’t just a leadership trait, but something everyone practices.
Organizations thrive when people recognize and value different working styles. Imagine regular team check-ins where people talk about how they like to work, or even switching up roles so folks can see things from a new angle. That kind of empathy and flexibility can make all the difference.
What does this look like in real life? Leaders can use personality mapping exercises, feedback sessions tailored to each color, and conflict resolution strategies that draw on color awareness.
When leaders model adaptability, it sets a tone. Suddenly, it’s not just okay—it’s encouraged for everyone to flex their own style and support each other. The result? A team that’s not just effective, but resilient, creative, and ready for anything.
